newsitem.title: USA: SBC long-distance bid runs into problems.
newsitem.headline: SBC long-distance bid runs into problems.

text.p: SBC Communications Inc's bid to become the first Baby Bell to enter the $80 billion long-distance business has run into problems, an Oklahoma state official said on Wednesday.

An Oklahoma regulator, in issuing a recommendation to the state's top phone regulators, said SBC has not met a crucial 14-point checklist of actions designed to open its local network to competitors, the official said.

Under last year's telecommunications law, the Bells must prove they have met the checklist before the Federal Communications Commission can allow them to offer long-distance service to local customers.
In making its decision, the FCC must consult with state regulators and the Justice Department. SBC last Friday applied to the FCC to offer long-distance service from Oklahoma.

An administrative law judge (ALJ) for the Oklahoma Corporation Commission (OCC), Robert Goldfield, held a hearing on the issue Tuesday, with SBC and rival long-distance carriers and others presenting testimony.
Goldfield, following the hearing, issued an oral recommendation to the OCC's three commissioners saying that SBC had not met the checklist.
"He recommended that (SBC) had not met the requirements of the 14-point checklist," said OCC spokesman Patrick Petree.
The spokesman added that Goldfield declined to go into detail about his recommendation. SBC is expected to appeal it at a hearing on April 23 before the three members of the OCC.
It is unclear how much weight the OCC will give Goldfield's recommendation.
Any recommendation the OCC makes will be forwarded to the FCC for its consideration. The OCC must issue a recommendation to the FCC by May 1 on whether SBC has met the checklist.
An SBC official was not immediately available to comment.

But a rival industry executive contended that SBC's "problems continue to mount. There are no residential customers in the state of Oklahoma receiving service from a competitor," the executive added, referring to one of the conditions for Bell entry into long distance. "As far as I'm concerned, their application is dead in the water."
An official for a unit of Brooks Fiber Properties Inc told the hearing Tuesday that the St. Louis-based company is not providing local phone service to residential customers.
SBC had contended to state regulators that Brooks was indeed providing such service, according to the Brooks official.

"We believe the application is extremely premature. We think it is unfortunate that (SBC) has felt compelled to file it at such an early stage. It puts the state and federal regulators under an unnecessary and time-consumer exercise," Edward Cadieux, director of regulatory affairs at Brooks, told Reuters.
Chicago-based Ameritech Corp was forced earlier this year to withdraw its FCC application for long-distance entry after it was discovered the document contained errors.
